JSON: Name: rgbx_diffusiondet_pipeline Title: Adaptive multimodal encoder for RGB-X object detection using DiffusionDet with dynamic channel reduction and multi-level aggregation Short Hypothesis: Integrating an auxiliary 2D modality X into the DiffusionDet framework by fusing RGB and X features in the encoder via dynamic channel reduction within CBAM and a dynamic multi-level aggregation block, while keeping the original DiffusionDet decoder unchanged, will increase object detection AP (AP50:95) on automotive RGB-X benchmarks compared to an RGB-only DiffusionDet baseline. Related Work: Existing multi-modal object detection approaches include one-stage and two-stage detectors that fuse RGB with depth, infrared, or other 2D/3D modalities. One-stage fusion methods emphasize runtime but often sacrifice accuracy and struggle with sparse or misaligned auxiliary inputs. Transformer- and CNN-based fusion schemes apply cross-attention or feature concatenation, but they typically use fixed channel projection and static multi-scale selection, limiting cross-modal adaptivity and leading to redundancy or modality domination under sensor degradation. Attention modules (e.g., channel and spatial attention variants) improve per-modality focus but are rarely conditioned dynamically on fused channel statistics. Diffusion-based object detection (DiffusionDet and extensions) refines box proposals iteratively; prior extensions address oriented or dense scenes but were developed for RGB only or required adapting decoder capacity when adding modalities. Polarimetric data has been explored for perception but lacks standardized pixel-aligned object detection datasets and integration strategies in diffusion-based detectors. In summary, prior work lacks a lightweight, input-conditioned encoder fusion mechanism that: (a) dynamically reduces redundant channels based on attention, (b) aggregates multi-scale fused features adaptively per proposal, and (c) preserves the original diffusion decoder capacity. Abstract: We address multimodal RGB-X object detection by proposing an encoder-side integration method compatible with diffusion-based detectors. The approach fuses auxiliary 2D modality X (e.g., depth, infrared, polarimetric) with RGB at the FPN level via a dynamic channel reduction conditioned on channel attention and a dynamic multi-level aggregation block that produces proposal-aligned multi-scale features. Two regularization terms enforce channel saliency and object-focused spatial selectivity to produce compact, discriminative embeddings. Crucially, only the encoder is modified; the DiffusionDet decoder and its iterative refinement capacity remain unchanged, preserving decoder complexity and maintaining comparable inference characteristics. The main contributions are: (1) an input-dependent channel reduction within an attention module to remove cross-modal redundancy; (2) a dynamic aggregation mechanism that selects and weights multi-scale fused features per proposal; and (3) regularizers that increase feature compactness and spatial alignment. The expected outcome is consistent AP improvements and greater robustness to RGB corruption across automotive RGB-X benchmarks without increasing decoder computational burden. Experiments: Datasets: (1) KITTI projected RGB-D: 6,733 training, 748 test images; (2) RGB-Polarimetric (pixel-aligned) dataset: 11,200 training, 1,427 test images (this work's annotated splits); (3) M3FD RGB-IR: 2,940 training, 1,260 test images. Baselines: (A) RGB-only DiffusionDet (original decoder, single-modality encoder); (B) adjusted multi-modal one-stage detector (e.g., YOLOv8n extended to RGB-X); (C) representative multimodal fusion state-of-the-art methods (SwinFusion, PIAFusion, CDDFuse or nearest published variants) reimplemented for parity. Metrics: primary: AP50:95 (COCO style), secondary: AP50, per-class AP, average inference time per image, and robustness score under corrupted RGB (delta AP relative to clean). Statistical protocol: report mean ± std over 5 independent runs with different seeds; apply paired t-test (alpha=0.05) vs RGB-only baseline. Implementation and training: ResNet50+FPN backbones per modality; number of proposal boxes N=500; train with AdamW on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU or equivalent; report wall-clock training time and peak GPU memory. Core experiments: 1) Main comparison: train and evaluate proposed encoder + original DiffusionDet decoder vs baselines on each dataset (report AP50:95, AP50, per-class AP). 2) Ablation study: incremental addition of (i) dynamic channel reduction CBAM (DCR-CBAM), (ii) channel-saliency regularizer, (iii) object-focused spatial regularizer, (iv) dynamic multi-level aggregation block (DMLAB). For each ablation measure AP and runtime. 3) Sensitivity study: vary reduced channel dimensionality C' in {96, 192, 224, 256, 320} and report AP and model parameter counts. 4) Diffusion iterations: evaluate performance vs decoder iterations in {1,3,10} for both baseline and proposed encoder to verify decoder capacity preservation. 5) Robustness tests: apply simulated RGB corruptions (black occlusion, salt-and-pepper, raindrop artifacts, depth-aware blur) at multiple severities and report delta AP and per-class impact. 6) Modal contribution analysis: measure normalized per-modality attention rates and PCA energy of fused features with/without regularizers; report quantitative shifts. 7) Runtime and scalability: measure average inference time per image and throughput for batch sizes {1,4,8}; report GPU memory. Preprocessing, augmentation, and hyperparameters follow consistent settings across comparisons; all models evaluated on the same test splits. One explicit ablation must compare the proposed encoder + unchanged decoder vs a variant that enlarges decoder capacity to process fused features, to isolate benefits of encoder-only fusion. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sensor alignment and calibration: misalignment between RGB and X (depth, IR, polarimetric) can degrade fused features and attention conditioning, producing incorrect dynamic reductions. 2) Data scarcity and annotation quality: the novel RGB-P dataset may have limited diversity and labeling noise, which can lead to overfitting or incorrect evaluation of polarimetric benefit. 3) Modality heterogeneity: the approach assumes pixel-aligned 2D modalities; extension to sparse or non-image modalities (e.g., LiDAR point clouds) requires additional preprocessing and may reduce effectiveness. 4) Decoder iteration cost: although decoder architecture is unchanged, required diffusion iterations for convergence may increase inference latency in high-accuracy regimes, limiting real-time applicability. 5) Regularizer sensitivity: channel and spatial regularizers require careful weighting; improper tuning can cause suppressed useful features or excessive sparsity and reduced generalization. 6) Compute and memory: added encoder fusion modules and per-input dynamic operators increase encoder FLOPs and memory, which may limit deployment on edge hardware. 7) Evaluation bias: automotive benchmarks used may not reflect all operational conditions (e.g., extreme weather or different camera models), limiting external validity. 8) Interpretability: dynamic attention-conditioned linear operators are input-dependent and may be harder to analyze or certify for safety-critical systems.
